newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN says airlift for Zaire refugees delayed again.
newsitem.headline: UN says airlift for Zaire refugees delayed again.

text.p: U.N. refugee agency efforts to help thousands of Rwandan Hutus stuck in Zaire ran into fresh snags on Friday when Tutsi-dominated rebels delayed a planned airlift and requisitioned the aviation fuel needed for it.

Rebels in the border town of Goma requisitioned 60,000 litres of aircraft fuel UNHCR was hoping to use for the refugee airlift from the regional hub, Kisangani. "We said 'you can have a few litres', they took the whole lot," said a UNHCR official.
In yet another blow, UNHCR suspended aid for up to 100,000 Rwandans south of rebel-controlled Kisangani after its staff were attacked by Zaireans angered by the presence of refugees.

An airlift of the first batch of refugee children out of Kisangani planned for Saturday was likely to be delayed further after local officials demanded further medical checks fearing a spread of cholera, UNHCR spokeswoman Pamela O'Toole said.

A total of 330 cholera cases and 19 cholera deaths have been registered amnong 50,000 refugees at Kasese camp, 29 km (17 miles) south of Kisangani. About 30,000 refugees are camped at another site and another 20,000 are scattered further south.
UNHCR and aid workers have been following the refugees deeper into Zaire as they flee with each rumoured rebel advance.
The agency's plan to take the refugees on trucks, planes and barges across the Zaire river back home has been repeatedly delayed amid mounting rebel formalities.

O'Toole said UNHCR wanted security guarantees from the rebels after the protest in Kisangani where hundreds of Zaireans prevented an aid convoy from leaving a ferry over the river, attacked vehicles and threatened aid workers.
She said rebel officials told the aid workers they could not go to the refugee camps unless they fed the local Zaireans.

A spokeswoman for the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) said Zaireans had in the last three days attempted to loot food aid from two warehouses in Kisangani and a train ferrying supplies to the refugees and local Zaireans living near the two camps.
Tensions were whipped up by aggressive local radio broadcasts against the refugees and unconfirmed reports in town that refugees had killed a rebel or several local Zaireans.
Aid workers, who declined to be identified, said they suspected rebels were inciting trouble to prevent the U.N. airlift of refugees via Kisangani.
The troubles do not stop at Zaire's borders.
Across the eastern frontier in Rwanda, the Tutsi-dominated Kigali government has told the UNHCR that it would like to screen all the refugees at the border, O'Toole said.
The refugees are the rump of more than two million Hutus who fled Rwanda in 1994 after the victory of Tutsi rebels in the civil war and the genocide of 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
Most returned home late last year but about 300,000 are believed to be stranded deeper in Zaire.
